summary: Defines the two metering and marking behaviors of PCN nodes, which protect the quality of service of inelastic flows in a Diffserv domain. Threshold metering marks packets once a load level is passed, with a second behavior as well.

plainLanguage.summary: Roads put up a warning sign when they get too crowded. This says how routers measure crowding and mark packets as a warning.

questions: what is pcn excess traffic marking
how does pcn admission control work
subtitle: How routers measure pre-congestion and mark packets as an early warning before queues build up.

tldr.problem: Real-time traffic with fixed bit rates cannot adapt to congestion, so a Diffserv domain needs an early warning that a link is nearly overloaded, before any significant queue builds up.
tldr.mechanism: Each PCN-node runs two token-bucket style meters on its PCN-traffic: a threshold-meter that marks all PCN-packets once traffic passes the PCN-threshold-rate, and an excess-traffic-meter that marks a share of packets equal to the rate above the PCN-excess-rate.
tldr.outcome: The level of marking lets PCN-boundary-nodes decide whether to admit a new flow or terminate existing ones. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is not obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 5670 is a Proposed Standard, published in November 2009, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the PCN metering and marking behaviours.

sections.title: Why Pre-Congestion Notification
sections.content:
Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) aims to protect the quality of service of inelastic flows inside a Diffserv domain in a simple, scalable and robust way. It uses two mechanisms: admission control, which decides whether to admit or block a new flow request, and, in abnormal circumstances, flow termination, which decides whether to end some existing flows.

To make those decisions the overall rate of PCN-traffic is metered on every link in the domain. PCN-packets are marked when certain configured rates are exceeded. Those rates sit below the link rate, so boundary nodes hear about overloads before any congestion occurs, which is where the name comes from.

RFC 5670 defines the two metering and marking behaviours that PCN-nodes follow. It notes that RFC 3168 defines a broadly RED-like default congestion marking behaviour but allows alternatives, and that this document defines one such alternative. The general PCN architecture is in RFC 5559.
sections.plainLanguage: Some traffic, like a phone call, cannot slow down when the road gets busy. So the road warns the people in charge early, before it is really jammed, and they can decide to let fewer calls in.

sections.title: The Functions in a PCN-Node
sections.content:
A PCN-interior-node is described as a chain of functions. The descriptions are functional and are not meant to restrict how a vendor builds them.

  • Behaviour aggregate (BA) classification decides whether an incoming packet is a PCN-packet.
  • Dropping (optional) drops packets if the link is overloaded.
  • The threshold-meter decides whether the bit rate of PCN-traffic exceeds the PCN-threshold-rate.
  • The excess-traffic-meter measures by how much the bit rate exceeds the PCN-excess-rate.
  • The marker actually marks PCN-packets when a meter says to.

Both meters work on all PCN-packets on the link, not on individual flows.

A node MUST classify a packet as a PCN-packet if its Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) and Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) fields match a PCN-enabled codepoint of the encoding scheme used in the domain. RFC 5696 defines the baseline encoding. A packet that is not a PCN-packet but shares the link and competes for forwarding bandwidth is a competing-non-PCN-packet, and it MUST NOT be PCN-marked.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet goes past a few helpers in a row. One checks if it belongs to the special group, two others count how busy the road is, and the last one stamps a warning on it if needed.

sections.title: The Two Meters
sections.content:
Both meters behave like a token bucket: sized in bits, filled at a configured reference rate, drained by the size in bits of each metered packet. A PCN-node MUST implement both, with behaviour functionally equivalent to the description.

The threshold-meter has fill F_tm, tokens added at the PCN-threshold-rate up to a maximum BS_tm, and tokens removed per packet down to zero. The bucket has a configured intermediate depth called threshold. If F_tm is below the threshold, the packet is to be threshold-marked. In effect, every PCN-packet is marked once the rate of PCN-traffic is above the PCN-threshold-rate.

The excess-traffic-meter has fill F_etm and is filled at the PCN-excess-rate up to BS_etm. It SHOULD mark independent of packet size ("packet size independent marking"). There, if the bucket is not negative, tokens are removed and the packet is not marked. If the bucket is negative, the packet is excess-traffic-marked and no tokens are removed. If that mode is not implemented, the meter MUST use the "classic" behaviour, where a packet is marked when the bucket is empty.

The excess-traffic-meter SHOULD NOT meter a packet that arrives already excess-traffic-marked, or one that this node drops.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a bucket that fills with tokens at a steady speed, and each packet takes some out. When the bucket gets too low, the router knows traffic is arriving faster than the bucket refills, so it marks packets.

sections.title: Dropping and Marking Rules
sections.content:
Dropping is optional (MAY). It works by metering all metered-packets and dropping some if the rate is higher than allowed. If a node drops PCN-packets, then packets that arrive already excess-traffic-marked SHOULD be preferentially dropped. The Appendix explains that this avoids over-termination with the "controlled load" edge behaviour when there are multiple bottlenecks. Only dropping is allowed: downgrading a packet to a lower priority aggregate is not, because it would lead to packet mis-ordering.

The marking function sets the packet's encoding state as the domain's encoding scheme specifies, and the same scheme MUST be used across the whole PCN-domain. A PCN-node MUST NOT mark a packet that is not a PCN-packet, turn a non-PCN-packet into a PCN-packet, or turn a PCN-packet into a non-PCN-packet.

Competing-non-PCN-packets MAY be metered, but they MUST NOT be PCN-marked.
sections.plainLanguage: Only packets in the special group may get a warning stamp, and nobody may move a packet in or out of the group. If the road is overloaded, packets that already carry a strong warning are the first to be thrown away.

sections.title: Implementation Notes
sections.content:
The informative appendices give example algorithms and comments. The example algorithms add tokens as min(BS, F + (now - lastUpdate) * rate) on each packet arrival, then either remove tokens or mark.

The appendices explain how the rates relate: the PCN-threshold-rate is configured below the rate allocated to the PCN traffic class, and PCN-excess-rate is greater than or equal to PCN-threshold-rate. Implementers have freedom, for example whether tokens are added at regular intervals or only when a packet is processed.

In general, having competing-non-PCN-traffic is not advised, because its unpredictable amount makes PCN less accurate. If it exists, it should be limited, for example by queueing it separately or dropping it above some rate.

The baseline encoding of RFC 5696 has only two encoding states, PCN-marked and not-marked. Both meters must still be implemented, and a deployment must choose consistently whether PCN-marked means excess-traffic-marked or threshold-marked.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipe says what the result must look like, not how to build the machine. Builders can choose how they do it as long as the same packets get the same warnings.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC assumes that all PCN-nodes are PCN-enabled and trusted to meter and mark truthfully. If not, there are many potential attacks. A rogue PCN-interior-node could mark all packets so that no flows are admitted, or mark none even when pre-congested.

PCN-interior-nodes are not flow-aware, which prevents some attacks that target specific flows in the data plane, such as denial of service or eavesdropping. PCN adds few specifics to general good practice in operational security (RFC 4778). For example, it may be sensible for a node to raise an alarm if it is persistently PCN-marking.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole system works only if every router tells the truth. A dishonest router could shout "full!" all the time or never warn anyone.
